persons.name: Josiah P Cook
persons.note: AN 1833 OR 1834 LIST — POLL, TAX OR MUSTER — WITH ANOTHER SOURCE. Read from directory_1843, directory_1844, tax_1833. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G2b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. tax_1833 stands against this person's name by 31 December 1833 and nothing says when they came. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Cook, J. P.” (tax_1833_021, line 73). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Cook' agrees with the entry's forenames; 5 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 1 time, as “COOK JOSIAH P”, 1833-10-25: 1 parcel of the school section — lot 7 of block 120 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $45.00 (ls0140). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: COOK JOSIAH P matches Josiah P Cook: the forename names Josiah P Cook of the 5 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Cook, Mrs. J. L. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0533, printed page 183), the roll printing neither when nor how the member was admitted. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Cook' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins J. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. THE SAME ROLL LINE IS MET BY OTHER TOWNSPEOPLE OF THIS NAME: second_presb_0533 is matched under this same rule to J. B. Cook (cook_j_b) and John Cook (cook_john), so it is met by three townspeople of this name, and it says which of them it was about no more than it says it was about this one — the test that decided it is a surname and a given initial agreeing, which cannot tell them apart. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

citations.citation: "Early Chicago Voter Lists" — the poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago (10 August 1833), the tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833, the election returns and poll list of 1834 filed 11 August 1834, and the 1835 poll list. Transcribed from the Illinois Regional Archives Depository originals by Ingrid Latimer Schulz, published in Chicago Genealogist XXV/4 (Summer 1993), and republished by the Genealogy Trails Transcription Team.

transcribes.work: Poll list for the first election of Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago (10 August 1833)
transcribes.note: 30 entries. Andreas says twenty-eight men voted at this election; the list prints thirty names. T-0542 searched for a count outside Andreas and found none — the Chicago Democrat did not exist until 26 November 1833 and its whole run to August 1835 carries no retrospective count of this poll — so the discrepancy STANDS, with the negative search recorded (claims/town_findings_voter_lists.json v004). On weight the thirty are the enrolments and Andreas's twenty-eight is an 1884 belief-statement ('It is believed') about the number of legal voters; neither count is repaired.

transcribes.work: Tax List of the Town of Chicago - 1833
transcribes.note: 115 entries. Names only — as published it carries no valuation, no lot and no figure, so it is not a ranked property roll (claims/town_findings_voter_lists.json v001).

transcribes.work: Election Returns - Poll List of 1834, filed 11 August 1834
transcribes.note: 115 entries. Andreas independently dates the second town election to 11 August 1834, which corroborates the list's own heading.

85 entries. THE LIST PRINTS NO DATE, AND IT IS NOT THE POLL BOOK OF THE THIRD TOWN ELECTION. That election is now dated from the town's own newspaper rather than from Andreas: the Chicago Democrat of 8 July 1835 announced the election of Trustees under the new charter for 'Friday of this week' and the issue of 15 July reported that it 'took place on Friday last' with the return — FRIDAY 10 JULY 1835, nine days after the 1835-07-01 scene date (claims/town_election_1835_democrat.json d001-d005). Andreas's town chapter, 'in July, 1835', is corroborated; his police chapter's 5 August 1835 is the day the newly elected board sat and passed the town's ordinance code over Hugunin's name as President. But that return gives single candidates 124 and 142 votes, which 85 men cannot cast, and six of the ten men who stood are absent from these 85 while the list runs unbroken from Adams to Wright — so this is a DIFFERENT poll, not a short printing of that one (claims/town_findings_voter_lists.json v003). Which poll is open; the county and state general election of Monday 3 August 1835 is the nearest candidate. Until it is settled, a name here evidences presence in Chicago in 1835 and not presence on any particular day.

what_it_supplies: 345 names of men who voted at, or were taxed by, the Town of Chicago in 1833, 1834 and 1835, as printed
which of the four lists each name stands on, and its position in that list
the courtesy and rank titles the lists print in front of a name (Col., Lt., Major, Dr.)

for the 1835 poll list: presence in Chicago during 1835, which is the strongest residence evidence this project holds short of a newspaper naming the man — but NOT presence on a stated day, because the list is undated and is shown not to be the poll book of the 10 July 1835 town election (T-0542)
what_it_does_not_supply: any address, street, lot or dwelling
any age, trade, household or family member
any date more precise than a list's own heading — and the 1835 list has no heading date at all
any woman, and any man who neither voted nor was taxed

what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.
Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.
A required distinction between named documentary landmarks and anonymous inferred infill.
what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.

citations.citation: The Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, June 1st, 1842, to June 1st, 1892 (Chicago: Knight, Leonard & Co., 1892), John C. Grant, editor — the semi-centennial volume of the congregation, read from the Princeton Theological Seminary copy digitised by the Internet Archive as item secondpresbyterian00chic
what_it_supplies: 2,255 lines of a Chicago church roll running from 1 June 1842 to 1892 — a name, how the member was admitted (profession or letter), the date, and for the closed roll a remark (dismissed, deceased, ordained).
962 distinct surnames, of which 938 lines carry a surname this project already holds from the town of 1835.
The founding cohort of 1 June 1842, which is where the overlap with the 1835 town is thickest: W. H. Brown, George W. Dole and Mrs A. N. Fullerton are all on the first day's roll.
A dated Chicago appearance for a surname, which is exactly the kind of second source the resident sweep files as a lead.
what_it_does_not_supply: An 1835 residency, or any part of one. The earliest line on the roll is seven years after the scene date and the ratified ladder never makes an 1835 resident from a later appearance alone.

A woman's own name, much of the time. The roll sets a wife as `Mrs.` followed by her HUSBAND'S name — `Fullerton, Mrs. A. N.` — so a line that meets a man in the 1835 layer has met his name and not him, and the crosswalk flags every such line.
A death or a departure that can be dated. `Deceased` and `Dismissed` are the state of the roll at its closing on 1 June 1892, not events with dates of their own.
An address, a trade or a household. The roll carries none of the three.
